task_description: Build Taskboard, an internal team task tracker. Two services: a Python 3.13 FastAPI REST API (/api/v1, OpenAPI) that is the only component talking to PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7 (cache-aside cache) and attachment storage (local filesystem in dev, Amazon S3 in AWS); and a Node.js 24 Express 5 + EJS UI server that renders pages, authenticates browser users and calls the API over an internal network. Features: register/login/logout with email+password, change password, forgot-password reset links (emails written to log and an outbox table), first admin created by a management command from env vars, admin user management (roles admin/member, deactivate/reactivate). Teams with owners and members added by email; projects inside teams (archive = read-only) with an optional outbound webhook URL that receives an async JSON POST with retry when a task changes status. Tasks with Markdown descriptions rendered as HTML, comments (Markdown), file attachments of any type up to 10 MB with download by original filename. Search across visible projects with free text, filters, client-supplied sort field and direction, pagination. CSV export of a project's tasks. Activity feed per project and global for admins. Deployed to AWS EC2 behind an ALB with Terraform (VPC, private subnets, RDS, ElastiCache, S3, ECR, IAM), Docker images bootstrapped via user_data.

threats.name: API keys or passwords are committed to the repo or baked into code
A user calls an admin or other-role function because only the UI hides it
Passwords are stored in plain text or with a fast hash, so a database leak exposes them
Sensitive data travels over plain HTTP or an unencrypted connection
Attackers try leaked or guessed passwords against your login at scale
Debug features or consoles are left on in production
Default or hardcoded admin accounts are left active
.env, .git, or backup files are reachable from the web
Encryption or signing keys are hardcoded or shared across environments
Password reset can be abused to take over accounts
Forged or unsigned JWTs are accepted
One user reads or changes another user's data by changing an id in the request
Session ids, reset tokens, or API keys can be guessed
A user grants themselves a higher role through a profile or signup request
Secrets are copied into the image or passed as build arguments
An attacker plants a session id before login and reuses it afterwards
Queries miss the tenant filter, so customers see each other's data
The coding agent can read .env files, SSH keys, or cloud credentials
Another website makes a logged-in user's browser perform actions
Session cookies can be read by scripts or sent over plain HTTP
A stolen password is enough to take over sensitive accounts
Old TLS or SSL versions or weak cipher suites are still enabled
Links in emails are built from the Host header, so attackers redirect reset links
Logout, password change, or account removal leaves sessions or tokens valid
Expired tokens or tokens meant for another service are accepted
Tokens in URLs or browser storage leak through logs, referrers, or scripts
Short or restricted passwords are easy to guess
Logins and access failures are not logged, so attacks go unnoticed
Login or reset responses reveal which emails have accounts

countermeasures.name: Load secrets from a secrets manager or environment
countermeasures.how_to: Keep secrets out of code, images, and the repo. Use environment variables or a vault, scope access narrowly, and rotate anything that leaked.

countermeasures.name: Check permissions on the server for every action
countermeasures.how_to: Enforce role and permission checks in a central layer on each endpoint, not only by hiding UI.

countermeasures.name: Hash passwords with a slow, salted algorithm
countermeasures.how_to: Use Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt through your framework's password helper. Never use MD5 or SHA for passwords.

countermeasures.name: Use HTTPS for every connection
countermeasures.how_to: Serve everything over HTTPS with a trusted certificate, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and use TLS for service-to-service calls as well.

countermeasures.name: Slow down repeated login failures
countermeasures.how_to: Throttle or temporarily lock after repeated failures per account and per IP, without making lockout itself a denial-of-service tool.

countermeasures.name: Reject known-breached passwords
countermeasures.how_to: Check new passwords against a breached-password list (for example the Pwned Passwords range API) at signup and change.

countermeasures.name: Offer or require a second factor
countermeasures.how_to: Support an authenticator app or passkeys, and require it for admins and sensitive actions.

countermeasures.name: Turn debug features off in production
countermeasures.how_to: Set DEBUG false, remove debug consoles and verbose logging, and fail the deploy if debug is on.

countermeasures.name: Remove default and hardcoded accounts
countermeasures.how_to: Ship no preset admin users. Create the first admin through a one-time setup step with a strong generated password.

countermeasures.name: Do not deploy repo metadata or env files
countermeasures.how_to: Exclude .git, .env, and backups from the build and the web root, and block them at the web server.

countermeasures.name: Use separate keys per environment and rotate them
countermeasures.how_to: Generate different keys for development, staging, and production, load them from the secrets manager, and rotate them on a schedule or after exposure.

countermeasures.name: Make password reset single-use and short-lived
countermeasures.how_to: Send a random single-use token that expires in minutes. Show the same response whether or not the account exists, and keep MFA in force.

countermeasures.name: Verify token signatures against an allow-list of algorithms
countermeasures.how_to: Verify every JWT signature, fix the accepted algorithms in code, and load keys from trusted configuration. Never accept alg none.

countermeasures.name: Check the user owns the object on every request
countermeasures.how_to: Look the object up by id AND owner, or check ownership explicitly, and return 404 when they do not match.

countermeasures.name: Generate tokens with a cryptographic random source
countermeasures.how_to: Use secrets.token_urlsafe, crypto.randomBytes, or the framework default. Never use Math.random, time, or counters.

countermeasures.name: Accept only the fields you expect
countermeasures.how_to: Bind requests to an explicit schema or DTO with allowed fields. Never copy a request body straight onto a model.

countermeasures.name: Issue a fresh session at login
countermeasures.how_to: Create a new session id on every login and re-authentication, and discard the old one.

countermeasures.name: Scope every query to the tenant
countermeasures.how_to: Apply the tenant filter in one place, such as a query helper or row-level security, so no query can forget it.

countermeasures.name: Keep secrets out of the agent's reach
countermeasures.how_to: Deny reads of .env files, SSH keys, and cloud credentials in the agent's permission rules, and use scoped short-lived credentials.

countermeasures.name: Protect state-changing requests from cross-site forgery
countermeasures.how_to: Use SameSite cookies plus anti-forgery tokens, and only change state with POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.

countermeasures.name: Set cookie security attributes
countermeasures.how_to: Use Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite on session cookies, preferably with the __Host- prefix.

countermeasures.name: Enable only current TLS versions and cipher suites
countermeasures.how_to: Allow TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, use the recommended cipher suites from your platform or proxy, and turn off SSL and older TLS.

countermeasures.name: Build links from a configured base URL
countermeasures.how_to: Take the public base URL from configuration, not from the Host or X-Forwarded headers of the request.

countermeasures.name: End sessions on the server
countermeasures.how_to: Invalidate server-side on logout, expiry, password change, and account removal. Do not rely on deleting the cookie client-side.

countermeasures.name: Check expiry, audience, and issuer
countermeasures.how_to: Reject expired tokens and tokens whose audience or issuer does not match your service.

countermeasures.name: Keep tokens and personal data out of URLs
countermeasures.how_to: Send tokens in headers or request bodies, never in query strings, which end up in logs and referrers.

countermeasures.name: Keep sensitive data out of browser storage
countermeasures.how_to: Prefer HttpOnly cookies for session tokens, and clear client-side data on logout.

countermeasures.name: Use length-based password rules
countermeasures.how_to: Require a minimum length (15 or more is better), allow long passphrases and any characters, and skip composition rules.

countermeasures.name: Log security-relevant events
countermeasures.how_to: Log logins, failures, permission denials, and admin actions with time, user, and source, and alert on spikes.

countermeasures.name: Return generic errors to users
countermeasures.how_to: Show a short message and a request id, log the details server-side, and use the same wording for unknown and wrong credentials.

also_consider.name: A request sets fields the user should not control, such as role or price
A user skips or repeats steps in a multi-step flow, such as verification or checkout
API responses include more fields than the client needs, such as hashes or internal ids
Unvalidated input reaches business logic and breaks assumptions
Attackers hammer an endpoint to brute-force, scrape, or run up your costs
A link on your domain sends users to an attacker-chosen site
Any website can read authenticated API responses because CORS allows every origin
Stack traces and internal details are shown to users

assessment.summary: 29 threats and 30 countermeasures for authentication, session-management, authorization, secrets-and-config, transport-security. Risk level critical (highest threat severity, raised for sensitive data).

instructions: Build these countermeasures in as you write the code, starting with the most severe threats. These threats come from the components you picked. also_consider lists general threats from implied components; pass those components explicitly for full detail. After writing code, call general_verify_code_security with the same components.
